title: The Vilna edition
hook: a printing in Vilna gave the Talmud page an address students everywhere share

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tosafot, and your line: additions. Rashi's grandsons and their students wrote questions along the outer edge of the page. Which commentary did you question? Today, the page they all sit on. Day one thousand one hundred two.

A message lands in a study group's chat: Berakhot two a, top of the page, can someone explain the third line? Within minutes three people answer. One is at a kitchen table, one is on a train, one is in a study hall full of noise. None of them has seen the others' books. Their copies were bought in different shops, in different years, maybe in different countries. And yet every one of them has the same words on the same line of the same page. Nobody had to ask which edition. That quiet agreement has a name and a hometown. Today's word is a city and a printing press.
screen: `BERAKHOT 2A, THIRD LINE.` → `THREE ANSWERS, THREE PLACES.` → `THE SAME LINE IN EVERY COPY.`

segments.voice: The Vilna edition. It's the printing of the Babylonian Talmud made in the city of Vilna, and its page became the standard page. Start with the address. A Talmud page is cited by tractate, by leaf, and by side. Each leaf has a front, side a, and a back, side b. So Berakhot two a means the tractate Berakhot, the second leaf, the front side. That's the address we used for the Gemara's opening question a few days ago. Second, the layout. You already know the shape: the center block, Rashi on the inside, Tosafot on the outside, small notes at the edges. On the Vilna page each of those voices has a fixed seat, and the same words sit in the same seat every time. Third, the numbering. Because later printings copy this page, a reference made in one city lands on the same words in another. That's what lets a whole community study one page together, a page a day, in what's called daf yomi, the daily page. Fourth, a small puzzle. A tractate's leaves begin with two, not one. Printers' history has its own explanation, and some readers like to add another: there is no first page, because no one ever begins at the very beginning. Someone was always learning before you. That's the Vilna edition. Not new words, but a shared map. The same page everywhere.
screen: `TRACTATE, LEAF, SIDE: AN ADDRESS.` · `GEMARA CENTER, RASHI IN, TOSAFOT OUT.` · `ONE PAGE, MANY PRINTINGS.` · `NO PAGE ONE.` · then, large: `THE SAME PAGE EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is finding a page by its number. If you have any book nearby, a Bible, a novel, a cookbook, pick a page number before you open it. Say it once. Then open straight to it, and look at the first line. Read it slowly, just that one line. If you have nothing nearby, hold a page address in your mind instead: a book, a leaf, a side. Now sit with the idea that somewhere, someone else is looking at that same line today. You don't know them. You share a page. Breathe in on the address, breathe out on the line. The bell holds the time.
The Vilna edition. The Talmud printing whose page layout and numbering later printings follow, so a reference finds the same words in any copy. Today's word.

Your line: the same page everywhere. Today, before you argue with someone, check that you're both on the same page, literally: the same text, the same line, the same facts. Then talk. Day one thousand one hundred two.

howItsDone: Students cite the Talmud by tractate, leaf and side, such as Berakhot 2a, and printed volumes that follow the Vilna layout share that numbering. Some communities study one page a day together in the daf yomi cycle.

original.note: Hebrew: a leaf of the Talmud, with two sides, a and b. Daf yomi means the daily page.

trapdoor: what you thought: one old edition of a book, among many.
what it means: the printing whose page later Talmuds copy, so every reference lands on the same words.
what a scholar hears: the Romm printing in Vilna, whose layout of Gemara, Rashi, Tosafot and marginal notes became the page students cite by leaf and side.
recall: from the lighter case to the heavier

notes: Under the claims rule, the index hook's date (the 1880s) and 'worldwide' were not stated; the city is named, the date left out. Keeper may wish to add a date if a cited source supports it.
Please confirm the layout description: Rashi on the inner margin, Tosafot on the outer, smaller notes (cross-references, later glosses) around them.
'Earlier printers had already set much of the page division, and the Vilna edition carried it forward' refers to the earlier Venice (Bomberg) printings; please confirm the phrasing.
The trapdoor names the Romm printing house; please confirm.
The explanation for tractates starting on leaf 2 is attributed to 'some readers' (a homiletic reading); the printers' own reason (the title page counted as leaf 1) is not stated as fact.
Daf yomi is described without dates or participant counts.
